key_terms.meaning: f is the number of observations in a value or class; Σf = n, the total number of observations.
A range of values with a lower limit L and upper limit U, used to group continuous data.
Classes such as 10–20, 20–30 where the upper limit is not included, so no value is counted twice.
Classes such as 10–19, 20–29 where both limits are included; convert by subtracting 0.5 from lower and adding 0.5 to upper limits.
A bar chart for grouped continuous data with touching bars whose heights are class frequencies.
A cumulative frequency curve; less-than ogive rises, more-than ogive falls, and their crossing estimates the median.
mean = Σx/n for raw data, where Σx is the sum of all observations and n is their count.
The middle value after sorting, or the average of the two middle values when n is even; it splits data into two equal counts.
The value or class with the highest frequency f; data can have no mode or more than one mode.
Range = maximum − minimum; it uses only two observations and ignores the rest.
QD = (Q₃ − Q₁)/2, where Q₁ and Q₃ are the first and third quartiles.
s = √(Σ(x − x̄)²/(n − 1)) for a sample; it measures typical distance from the mean in original units.
CV = (s / x̄) × 100%; it compares spread after removing the scale of the mean.
Skewness = (Q₃ + Q₁ − 2Q₂)/(Q₃ − Q₁), where Q₂ is the median; positive means a right tail.
A measure of tail heaviness and peakedness; excess kurtosis = kurtosis − 3 for the normal curve.
r = Σ(x − x̄)(y − ȳ) / √(Σ(x − x̄)² Σ(y − ȳ)²), with −1 ≤ r ≤ +1.
Spearman rₛ = 1 − 6Σd²/(n(n² − 1)), where d is the difference in ranks and n is the number of pairs.
The least-squares line y = a + bx predicting y from x; b is the slope and a is the intercept.
y = β₀ + β₁x₁ + β₂x₂ + … + ε, where each βⱼ is the change in mean y for a one-unit change in xⱼ holding others fixed.
ln(p/(1 − p)) = β₀ + β₁x, where p is the probability of a yes outcome; p must lie between 0 and 1.

takeaways: A frequency table turns raw observations into class counts, and every graph or statistic in this unit starts from that table.
The mean is the balance point, the median is the middle count and the mode is the most frequent value; choose by data type and outliers.
Standard deviation and quartile deviation measure spread in original units, while variance is in squared units.
CV = SD/mean × 100% lets you compare spread across groups with different units or very different means.
Skewness describes left-right asymmetry; kurtosis describes tail weight, not just the height of the peak.
Pearson r measures linear association only; rank correlation works with ordered data and reduces the effect of outliers.
Regression predicts one variable from another; the y-on-x and x-on-y lines differ unless correlation is perfect.
Multiple regression adds predictors and needs coefficient interpretation holding other variables fixed; logistic regression models a yes/no probability with an S-curve.
bank_note: Long answers usually ask for definitions, a worked table or calculation, interpretation of the statistic, and a clear statement of assumptions or limits.

bank.q: Define a frequency distribution. Explain exclusive and inclusive class intervals, and show how an inclusive table is converted for drawing a histogram.
outline: Frequency distribution as classes with counts f and total Σf = n
Exclusive classes: upper limit not included
Inclusive classes: both limits included; correction by 0.5
Effect of correction on class boundaries and histogram bars

bank.q: State the formulas for mean, median and mode for raw data. Explain why the median is preferred for income data with a few very large values.
outline: Mean = Σx/n with symbols defined
Median by sorting and middle position
Mode as most frequent value
Outliers pull the mean but leave the median stable

bank.q: Define range, quartile deviation and standard deviation. Give one practical situation where each is useful.
outline: Range = maximum − minimum; quick but uses two values
Quartile deviation uses Q₁ and Q₃ and ignores extreme tails
Standard deviation uses all observations and keeps original units
Situations: quality check, income spread, marks consistency

bank.q: Explain coefficient of variation and Bowley's coefficient of skewness. What does a positive skewness mean for a marks distribution?
outline: CV = (SD/mean) × 100% for relative spread
Bowley formula with Q₁, Q₂, Q₃
Positive skewness means a longer right tail
Few very high marks pull the mean above the median

bank.q: Define Karl Pearson correlation coefficient and Spearman rank correlation. State the range of each and one limitation.
outline: Pearson r formula and −1 ≤ r ≤ +1
Spearman formula using rank differences d
Pearson measures linear association only
Rank correlation handles ordinal data but loses some information

bank.q: Given a grouped frequency table of daily UPI transaction amounts, construct less-than and more-than ogives and estimate the median from their intersection.
outline: Cumulative frequencies for both ogives
Correct class boundaries and axes
Intersection gives an estimate of the median
Comment on the estimate against the grouped median formula

bank.q: A sample of 10 workers' monthly earnings has mean ₹18,000 and standard deviation ₹2,500. Compute the coefficient of variation and interpret it.
outline: Numerical answer with % unit
Small CV means earnings are relatively consistent
CV allows comparison with another group having a different mean

bank.q: For paired data on advertising spend and sales, compute Karl Pearson r from summary sums and fit the line of y on x.
outline: Use r formula with Σx, Σy, Σxy, Σx², Σy²
Substitute and simplify carefully
Slope b = Σ(x − x̄)(y − ȳ)/Σ(x − x̄)²
Intercept a = ȳ − b x̄ and write y = a + bx

bank.q: Two judges rank 8 contestants. Compute Spearman rank correlation and comment on the agreement between the judges.
outline: Assign ranks and find d for each contestant
Compute Σd²
Apply rₛ = 1 − 6Σd²/(n(n² − 1)) with n = 8
Interpret near +1 as strong agreement

bank.q: Fit a multiple regression with two predictors using given normal equations, and interpret each coefficient.
outline: Write the model y = β₀ + β₁x₁ + β₂x₂ + ε
Set up or use the normal equations
Solve for β₀, β₁, β₂
Interpret β₁ holding x₂ fixed, and β₂ holding x₁ fixed

bank.q: In a loan-default data set, explain how you would fit and interpret a logistic regression with one predictor, including the odds ratio.
outline: Code default as 1 and no default as 0
Model ln(p/(1 − p)) = β₀ + β₁x
Convert a coefficient to odds ratio exp(β)
Predicted probability stays between 0 and 1

bank.q: A company reports mean salary ₹50,000 and SD ₹5,000; another reports mean ₹80,000 and SD ₹12,000. Compare the relative variability and discuss which group has more unequal salaries.
outline: CV₁ = 10%, CV₂ = 15%
Higher CV means greater relative spread
Absolute SD is larger in the second group
Compare only after scaling by the mean

bank.q: Explain why the regression line of y on x and x on y are different. Show how r² measures the fraction of variation explained.
outline: Minimising vertical errors gives y on x
Minimising horizontal errors gives x on y
Both lines pass through (x̄, ȳ)
r² = explained variation/total variation; 0 ≤ r² ≤ 1

bank.q: Compare a linear probability model with logistic regression for a yes/no outcome. Discuss predicted probabilities, coefficient interpretation and one diagnostic check.
outline: Linear model can predict below 0 or above 1
Logistic model keeps p in (0,1) through the S-curve
Coefficients act on log-odds, not directly on p
Check calibration or use a confusion table and ROC curve

glossary.def: Recorded observations such as marks, prices or counts.
A characteristic that changes from one observation to another.
Labels with no order, such as city names or payment app names.
Labels with a meaningful order, such as poor, average and good.
A line graph joining class midpoints with heights equal to frequencies.
The running total of frequencies up to a class boundary.
The midpoint of a class interval, used as a representative value.
A chart with separated bars whose lengths show counts or amounts.
The sum of observations divided by their number.
The middle value of ordered data.
The most frequent value or class.
The amount by which values spread away from a centre.
The average squared distance from the mean.
The square root of variance, in the original units.
A value that cuts ordered data into four equal-count parts.
A plot of paired values that shows the direction of association.
A number from −1 to +1 that measures linear association.
A method that predicts one variable from one or more other variables.
Choosing coefficients that minimise the sum of squared residuals.
The difference between an observed value and its predicted value.
The ratio p/(1 − p), where p is the probability of an event.
The S-shaped function 1/(1 + e^(−z)) that turns a score into a probability.
A measure of left-right asymmetry in a distribution.
A measure of tail weight and peakedness relative to a normal curve.
A value below which a given percentage of observations fall.
A value far from the main body of the data.
